* **Typography & Styling:** Customize fonts, text alignment, spacing, and effects.

* **Interactivity:** Use pseudo-classes, transitions, and transforms to animate and enhance user experience.
* **Responsive Design:** Create websites that look great on all devices using media queries.

**Get ready to turn your HTML knowledge into beautiful, functional websites with CSS!**

pages.title: Introduction to CSS - The Language of Style
pages.content:
- **CSS**, which stands for **C**ascading **S**tyle **S**heets, is the language that adds style to your HTML.
If HTML is like the framework of a house, CSS is the paint, furniture, and decorations. HTML gives your webpage its structure, while CSS gives it its appearance.



---
**The Role of CSS**

The main job of CSS is to control the way your website looks. This includes:
* **Colors:** Changing the colors of text, backgrounds, and buttons.
* **Layout:** Deciding where elements go on the page. Do you want things side-by-side or stacked on top of each other?
* **Fonts:** Choosing different font styles, sizes, and weights for your text.

The best practice is to keep your CSS separate from your HTML. This makes your code more organized and efficient. For example, if you want to change the color of all the headings on your website, you can do it with just one line of code in your CSS file.

Now you have a basic understanding of what CSS is for. In the next lesson, we will start learning about how to write CSS and connect it to your HTML files.

pages.title: Applying CSS - Inline
pages.content:
- When you want to quickly style just one element on a webpage, you can use **inline CSS**.  
- With inline CSS, the style is written **directly inside the HTML tag** using the `style` attribute.  
Think of it like writing a sticky note on one element saying “Hey, look different!”.

**Good for:** quick changes, testing, or when you only need to style one element.  
**Not good for:** large projects, because your HTML becomes messy and hard to manage.

pages.title: CSS Syntax
pages.content:
- CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) uses a simple and consistent **syntax** to style HTML elements. Every CSS rule has **three main parts**:



---
**1. Selector**
- The **selector** tells the browser *which HTML element(s)* you want to style.\
 Example: `p` selects all `` tags.\
 Example: `.title` selects all elements with class="title".

**2. Property**
- The **property** defines *what aspect* of the element you want to style.\
  Examples: `color`, `font-size`, `background`, `margin`.

**3. Value**
- The **value** specifies *how the property should be applied*.\
  Examples: `red`, `20px`, `center`, `bold`.

---
**Example Rule**

```css
p {
   color: blue;
   font-size: 18px;
}
```

This means: *"Make all `` text blue, with a font size of 18px."*

pages.title: CSS Selectors
pages.content:
- You've already learned to use a simple **element selector**, like `p`, to style every single paragraph on a page. That's great for global changes, but what if you want to style some paragraphs differently from others? Or what if you want to target a single, unique element?
- To do that, you need to use more specific selectors. This is where **universal**, **class**, and **ID** selectors come in. They give you the power to target and style elements with precision.

---
**1. The Element Selector (`p`,`h1`, `div`)**\
This is the selector you already know. It targets all elements of a specific type.

* **When to use it:** To style every instance of a specific HTML tag. For example, to make all `` tags blue or all `` links a certain color.
* **Syntax:** Just the name of the HTML tag.\
CSS
```css
p {
  color: darkgreen;
}
```
---

**2. The Class Selector (`.`)**\
Think of a class as a **category**. You can give a class name to as many HTML elements as you want. Any element that has that class name will receive the styles you apply to it.

* **When to use it:** To style **multiple elements** that share a common purpose or appearance. For example, you might have a class called `highlight` to make certain words stand out, or a class called `card` to style a group of different boxes on your page.
* **Syntax:** You start the selector with a period (`.`) followed by the class name you choose.

CSS

```css
.card {
  background-color: lightgray;
}
```
---
**3. The ID Selector (`#`)**\
Think of an ID as a **unique identifier**, like a Social Security number. An ID can only be used **once** on an entire web page.

* **When to use it:** To style a **single, unique element**. You might use an ID for a main navigation bar, a specific logo, or a hero image that only appears once.
* **Syntax:** You start the selector with a hash symbol (`#`) followed by the ID name you choose.

CSS

```css
#main-heading {
  font-size: 32px;
  color: navy;
}
```
---
**4. The Universal Selector (`*`)**\
Think of the universal selector as a way to select **everything**. It is the most general selector and is often used to apply a style to all elements on the page.

* **When to use it:** To apply a default style to every element, such as setting a consistent font, or to reset padding and margins at the beginning of a stylesheet.
* **Syntax:** It is a single asterisk (`*`).

CSS

```css
* {
  font-size: 16px;
}
```

pages.title: CSS Box Model
pages.content:
- You've learned to style elements with colors, fonts, and borders. Now, it's time to understand the most fundamental concept in CSS: **The Box Model**.
- The Box Model explains how every single HTML element—from a `` to a `` tag—is treated as a rectangular box by the browser. This model determines an element's total size and how it takes up space on the page.
---
Think of it like a gift box with four layers:

1. **Content:** This is the innermost layer. It's the actual content of the element, such as your text or an image.
2. **Padding:** This is the empty space **inside** the box, between the content and the border. It's like the protective packing material that adds breathing room around the content.
3. **Border:** This is the line that wraps around the padding and content. It's the physical box itself.
4. **Margin:** This is the empty space **outside** the box. It separates the element from other elements on the page, like the empty space on a table between your gift box and another item.



---
**The order always goes from the inside out:**
`Content` → `Padding` → `Border` → `Margin`

- Understanding these four layers is key to controlling the size, spacing, and layout of every element on your web page.

pages.title: CSS Borders - Style Your Elements
pages.content:
- You've already used a simple `border` as part of the Box Model. You know it adds a line around an element. Now, let's look at how you can make your borders much more creative and interesting.
- Borders are made up of three parts: a **width**, a **style**, and a **color**. By changing these properties, you can create a wide variety of effects.

**Border Style**

This property is the most powerful. It defines what your border actually looks like. Some common styles are:

* `solid`: A single, solid line (the one you've used so far).
* `dotted`: A border made of dots.
* `dashed`: A border made of dashes.
* `double`: Two solid lines right next to each other.

---
**Border-Radius**
- This property is what you use to create rounded corners. Instead of a sharp, square corner, you can give your boxes soft, curved edges.
- The value of `border-radius` controls how much the corners are rounded. A larger number creates a more rounded corner. Using `border-radius: 50%` is a simple trick to create a perfect circle or oval from a square or rectangle.

By combining these properties, you can give your elements a professional and polished look.

```css
.notification { border: 2px solid #2563eb; border-radius: 8px; }
```

pages.title: CSS Display Property
pages.content:
- You have learned how to style your boxes with colors, padding, and borders. Now, let's learn how to control how those boxes arrange themselves on the page.
- The `display` property is one of the most important in CSS. It defines the fundamental "type" of an element, which controls how it acts in relation to other elements. Think of it as an element's basic rule for how it appears and takes up space.

---
Here are the four most common values:

* **`display: block;`** (The Stacker):
   * This is the default for elements like ``, ``, and ``.
   * Block elements always start on a **new line**.
   * They take up the **full available width** of their parent, like a giant invisible wall, forcing the next element below it.

* **`display: inline;`** (The Flow-er):
   * This is the default for elements like `` and ``.
   * Inline elements sit on the **same line** as other content.
   * They only take up as much width as their content needs.
   * **You cannot** set a `width` or `height` on an inline element.

* **`display: inline-block;`** (The Best of Both Worlds):
   * This is a special value that combines the best of both types.
   * Like an inline element, it sits on the **same line** as other elements.
   * But, like a block element, you **can** set a `width`, `height`, and all sides of `margin` and `padding`. This makes it a powerful tool for arranging elements side-by-side.

* **`display: none;`** (The Disappear-er):
   * This value makes an element completely **invisible**.
   * It removes the element from the page layout entirely, and it takes up **no space**.
---

pages.title: CSS - Height and Width
pages.content:
- You have learned to style the borders and spacing of your elements. Now, let's learn how to control their exact size.
- The `height` and `width` properties control how tall and how wide an element is. They are most commonly used on `block` and `inline-block` elements.
---
**Pixels (`px`)**\
This gives you a **fixed, exact size**. A `200px` width will always be 200 pixels wide, no matter the screen size. Use pixels when you need a very specific, unchanging dimension.

**Percentages (`%`)**\
This gives you a **flexible, relative size**. A percentage is based on the size of the element's parent container. For example, `width: 50%;` will make the element take up exactly half the width of the box it's inside.

**`auto`**\
This is the **default** value. It tells the browser to automatically calculate the size based on the element's content. For example, a paragraph's height will grow or shrink to fit all its text.

---

```css
.media { width: 100%; max-width: 480px; height: 240px; }
```

pages.title: CSS Overflow
pages.content:
- You have learned how to give your elements a specific `height` and `width`. But what happens when you put more content inside a box than it can hold? The content will overflow its container.
- The `overflow` property tells the browser what to do with this extra content. Think of it as deciding what to do with items that don't fit in a fixed-size box.

---
**Three Main Values for the Overflow Property**

**1.`overflow: hidden;`** (The Chopper)
- This value simply cuts off any content that goes beyond the edges of the container. The overflowing content will be invisible and completely inaccessible.
* **Use case:** When you want to ensure your layout stays clean and nothing spills outside of a specific area.

**2.`overflow: scroll;`** (The Scroller)
- This value adds a scrollbar to the container, whether the content needs it or not. The user can then scroll to see the hidden content.

* **Use case:** When you always want a scrollbar to appear in a certain area for a consistent design.

**3.`overflow: auto;`** (The Smart Scroller)
- This is the most common and often best choice. It is smart because it only adds a scrollbar **if and when** the content actually overflows the container.

* **Use case:** When you want to allow scrolling for long content without showing a scrollbar for short content, creating a cleaner look.

```css
.comments { max-height: 280px; overflow-y: auto; }
```

pages.title: CSS Backgrounds - Colors and Images
pages.content:
- When building a webpage, the **background** sets the tone and feel. CSS lets you change the background of any element using **solid colors** or **images**.

**1. `background-color`**: 
This property fills the background of an element with a solid color.

* You can use color names (`red`, `blue`), HEX codes (`#ff0000`), RGB (`rgb(255,0,0)`), or HSL (`hsl(0, 100%, 50%)`).

**Example:**

```css
p {
  background-color: lightblue;
}
```

This makes every paragraph have a light blue background.

---
**2. `background-image`**:
This property sets an image as the background of an element.

* The image repeats by default to fill the space.
* You can combine it with other properties (like `background-repeat`, `background-size`) to control how it looks.

**Example:**

```css
body {
  background-image: url("pattern.png");
}
```

This adds a repeating pattern image to the page background.

pages.title: font-family Property
pages.content:
- The `font-family` property specifies which font to use for text. It works as a priority list, moving from the first choice to fallbacks if a font isn’t available.

**Example**
```sdfw
p { font-family: "Helvetica", Arial, sans-serif; }
```
- Tries **Helvetica** first → then **Arial** → finally a generic **sans-serif**.  
- Always end with a generic font family to ensure readability.

---
**Types of Font Names in `font-family`**

**1.Specific Font Names**
- These are exact fonts, like `Arial`, `"Times New Roman"`, or `"Courier New"`.  
- If a font name has spaces, you must use quotes:
```css
h1 { font-family: Georgia, serif; } /* no quotes needed /
p { font-family: "Times New Roman", serif; } / quotes required */
```

**2.Generic Font Families**\
These are broad categories that act as a final fallback:  
- **serif**: Fonts with small strokes at the ends of letters (e.g., Times New Roman). They feel traditional or formal.  
- **sans-serif**: Fonts without strokes (e.g., Arial, Helvetica). They look clean, modern, and easy to read on screens.  

Always end your list with a generic family. This guarantees your text is displayed in a readable style, even if the specific fonts aren’t available.

pages.title: Font Size & Readability
pages.content:
- When you write text on a website, it's important that people can **read it easily**. Two CSS properties help with this:

**1.font-size**\
Decides **how big or small** the text looks.
Can be written in:
* **px (pixels)** → fixed size (e.g., `16px`)
* **% (percent)** → size compared to its parent text
* **em / rem** → size that can change depending on the base font

**Example:**

```css
p {
  font-size: 18px;   /* This text will look a little bigger */
}
```
---
**2.line-height**\
Decides the **space between lines** of text.
* Makes text **comfortable** to read.
* Usually written as a number like `1.5`, which means *1.5 times the font size*.

**Example:**

```css
p {
  font-size: 18px;
  line-height: 1.5;   /* Gives breathing space between lines */
}
```
---
**Why Use Both?**

* `font-size` = how big the letters are.
* `line-height` = how much space is between lines.
* Together, they make text **clear, balanced, and easy to read**.

pages.title: Styling Font Weight & Spacing
pages.content:
- When you style text, it’s not just about the font family or size - how bold or spaced out the text looks also affects readability and design. CSS gives you properties to control this:

1. **font-weight**  
Controls how bold or light the text appears.  
Common values:  
- `normal` → default weight  
- `bold` → makes text thicker  
- Numbers like `100`, `400`, `700` → fine-tuned control (`400` = normal, `700` = bold).  

Example:  
```sd
h1 {
font-weight: bold;
}
```
---
2. **letter-spacing**  
- Controls the space between individual letters.  
- Useful for titles, headings, or creating a more “open” look.  

Example:  
```asdf
h2 {
letter-spacing: 2px;
}
```
---
3. **word-spacing**  
- Controls the space between words.  
- Helps improve readability or create stylistic effects.  

Example:  
```sdfef
p {
word-spacing: 8px;
}
```

pages.title: Text Alignment & Transformation
pages.content:
- When styling text in CSS, **how text is positioned and how it looks** can make a big difference in readability and design. Two very useful properties for this are:

**1. Text Alignment (`text-align`)**

This property controls **where the text sits** inside its container.

* `left` → Aligns text to the left (default in most languages).
* `center` → Places text in the middle.
* `right` → Aligns text to the right.
* `justify` → Stretches text so that both left and right edges are neat (like newspapers).

**Use case**: Aligning titles to the center, making navigation menus right-aligned, or using justify for long paragraphs.

---
**2. Text Transformation (`text-transform`)**

This property changes **the case (uppercase/lowercase)** of text without rewriting the content.

* `uppercase` → Turns all letters into CAPITALS.
* `lowercase` → Makes all letters small.
* `capitalize` → Makes the first letter of each word uppercase.

**Use case**: Creating professional-looking headings, consistent button labels, or emphasizing important words.

pages.title: Decorations & Effects in CSS
pages.content:
- So far, you've learned how to style text with fonts, size, alignment, and spacing. But what if you want to **add extra visual effects** to make your text stand out?
- That's where **text-decoration** and **text-shadow** come in!

**1.`text-decoration`**\
This property is used to **add or remove lines** from text.

* `underline` → adds a line under the text.
* `overline` → adds a line above the text.
* `line-through` → draws a line across the text (like crossing it out).
* `none` → removes any decoration.

**Example:**

```css
p {
  text-decoration: underline;
}
```
---
**2.`text-shadow`**\
This property lets you add a **shadow effect** behind your text. It takes **4 values**:

* Horizontal shadow (x-axis)
* Vertical shadow (y-axis)
* Blur (softness of shadow)
* Color

**Example:**

```css
h1 {
  text-shadow: 2px 2px 5px gray;
}
```

This would make the heading look like it has a **soft gray shadow** behind it.

pages.title: CSS Positioning - static and relative
pages.content:
- The **position** property in CSS decides how an element is placed on the page. By default, every element follows the normal flow of the document - one after another, top to bottom. But with positioning, you can shift elements around in more flexible ways.
---
1. **position: static; (The Default)**  
   - This is the **default value** for all elements.  
   - The element stays in the **normal document flow** (stacked like blocks or inline as usual).  
   - You **cannot move it** with `top`, `left`, `right`, or `bottom` properties.  
   - Think of it as: “Just stay where the page naturally puts you.”  
   - Example: A paragraph with `position: static;` will appear right after the previous element, like normal text.

2. **position: relative; (The Shifter)**  
   - The element still **stays in the document flow** (it takes up its normal space).  
   - But you can now **shift it** using `top`, `left`, `right`, or `bottom`.  
   - Importantly: The space it originally occupied is **still reserved**.  
   - Think of it as: “Stay in your place, but move a little without disturbing others.”  
   - Example: A box with `position: relative; top: 20px; left: 10px;` will look like it has “slid” down and to the right - but the space it left behind is still there.
---

pages.title: Absolute & Fixed Positioning
pages.content:
- CSS positioning lets you place elements exactly where you want them.  
- Now we’ll explore **absolute** and **fixed**, which give you much more control than static or relative.
---
1. **position: absolute; (The Breakaway)**  
   - The element is **removed from the normal document flow** (it no longer reserves space).  
   - It is positioned **relative to its nearest positioned ancestor** (the closest parent with `position: relative`, `absolute`, or `fixed`).  
   - If no such ancestor exists, it positions itself relative to the entire **page (document body)**.  
   - You can use `top`, `left`, `right`, and `bottom` to place it exactly where you want.  
   - Example:  A box with `position: absolute; top: 20px; left: 30px;` will float **20px from the top** and **30px from the left** of its positioned container (or the page if no parent is positioned).

2. **position: fixed; (The Sticker)**  
   - The element is also **removed from the normal flow**.  
   - It is positioned **relative to the viewport** (the visible screen area), not to a parent.  
   - This means it **stays in the same place even when you scroll**.  
   - Great for making sticky headers, navigation bars, or “back to top” buttons.  
   - Example: A button with `position: fixed; bottom: 10px; right: 10px;` will always stay in the **bottom-right corner** of the screen, no matter how much you scroll.

pages.title: Position - Sticky
pages.content:
- Sticky positioning is a mix between relative and fixed.  
- An element with `position: sticky` behaves like relative until you scroll past a certain point, then it sticks to a position like fixed.  
- This is useful for headers, table headings, or navigation bars that you want to remain visible only after scrolling to a certain point.
---
**Key Points:**

- It requires a `top`, `bottom`, `left`, or `right` value to define where it sticks.  
- It stays within its parent container, unlike fixed which is relative to the viewport.  
- Until the element reaches the sticky point, it behaves like a normal relative element.

**Use Cases:**
- A table header that stays visible while scrolling through rows.  
- A sidebar that becomes fixed when you scroll down a long page.
---
**Syntax:**
```dfwef
.sticky-element {
position: sticky;
top: 10px; /* sticks 10px from the top when scrolling */
}
```

pages.title: Z-Index & Stacking Order
pages.content:
- When you have **multiple elements overlapping** on a page, which one appears on top? That’s where **z-index** comes into play.  
- Think of your elements like **cards stacked on a table**.  
  - The card on top is fully visible.  
  - The cards underneath are partially or completely hidden.  
- In CSS, **z-index** controls which “card” is on top.
---
**Key Points:**

**1.Higher Z-Index = On Top**  
  - Elements with a higher `z-index` value appear **above** elements with a lower value.  
  - Example: `z-index: 10` will appear above `z-index: 5`.

**2.Position Matters**  
  - `z-index` only works on elements that have `position` set to `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, or `sticky`.  
  - Static elements ignore `z-index`.

**3.Stacking Context**  
  - Each positioned element can create a **stacking context**, which is like a mini-layered world inside itself.  
  - Elements in one stacking context don’t automatically stack with elements outside of it.
---
**Example**\
Imagine three boxes: **Red**, **Green**, **Blue**.  
- If all boxes are overlapping, the one with the **highest z-index** will appear on top.  
- If two boxes have the same z-index, the one that appears **later in HTML** will be on top.

pages.title: Flex Container & Flex Items
pages.content:
- Flexbox (short for **Flexible Box Layout**) is one of the most powerful tools in CSS for arranging elements.  
- Instead of struggling with floats, margins, or positioning, Flexbox lets you easily align and distribute space between elements.

---
**Flex Container**\
To start using Flexbox, you first declare a parent element as a **flex container**.
```sdfwef
.container {
display: flex;
}
```
- This makes `.container` a **flex container**.  
- All the direct child elements inside it automatically become **flex items**.
---
**Flex Items**\
The elements inside the flex container are called **flex items**.  
- They sit next to each other in a row by default.  
- They can stretch, shrink, or align depending on the container’s settings.
---
**Controlling Layout with Flexbox**
- **justify-content** → controls how items are spaced horizontally (main axis).
  - Example: justify-content: space-around; spreads items evenly with space around them.
- **align-items** → controls how items are aligned vertically (cross axis).
  - Example: align-items: center; centers items vertically inside the container.

Together, these two properties give you precise control over positioning without needing extra hacks.

pages.title: Flex Sizing
pages.content:
- Flexbox not only helps arrange items but also controls how much space each item takes inside a container. This is where flex sizing comes in.
---
1. **flex-grow**  
Determines how much an item can grow relative to other items when there’s extra space in the container.  
Example: `flex-grow: 2;` → this item will grow twice as much as an item with `flex-grow: 1`.

2. **flex-shrink**  
Determines how much an item can shrink relative to other items when space is limited.  
Example: `flex-shrink: 0;` → this item won’t shrink even if the container gets smaller.

3. **flex-basis**  
Sets the initial size of a flex item before growing or shrinking.  
Can be in pixels, percentages, or auto.  
Example: `flex-basis: 200px;` → the item starts at 200px, then grows or shrinks based on available space.
---
**Shorthand: flex**\
You can combine all three properties in one line:
```dfwef
.item {
flex: 1 0 200px; /* flex-grow | flex-shrink | flex-basis */
}
```

- `1` → grow factor  
- `0` → shrink factor  
- `200px` → initial size

pages.title: Grid Container & Items
pages.content:
- CSS Grid is a layout system that helps you place items in **rows and columns** at the same time. It’s like giving your page a neat table-like structure, but with way more flexibility.

**1. The Grid Container**
- To start, you need a **parent element** that holds your grid. You turn it into a grid with:
```wdfw
.container {
display: grid;
}
```
Once you do this, all the direct children inside become **grid items**.

----
**2. Defining Rows and Columns**
- The most important part of Grid is deciding how many **rows** and **columns** you want:
```wdweqcd
.container {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 200px 200px 200px; /* 3 columns */
  grid-template-rows: 100px 100px;          /* 2 rows */
  /* You can also use repeat() to shorten this, e.g., grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 200px); */
}

```

This gives you a grid with **3 columns** and **2 rows**.  
- Each column is **200px** wide.  
- Each row is **100px** tall.  
- Items will automatically fill these cells one after another.
---
**3. Grid Items**
- Any child element inside the grid container becomes a **grid item**.  
- By default, they fill the cells **from left to right, top to bottom**, like this:
```wdcw
1 | 2 | 3
4 | 5 | 6
```

pages.title: CSS Transitions
pages.content:
- Have you ever noticed how a button or link on a website might smoothly change color instead of just "popping" to a new color? That's a CSS transition at work!
- Transitions allow you to control the speed of a change in a CSS property, making the animation smooth and professional. They bring your static designs to life and improve the user experience.

---
**Core Properties**
- A CSS transition is made up of four main properties. You need at least the first two for a transition to work.

**1. `transition-property`**
* **What it does:** Specifies the CSS property you want to animate.
* **Example:** `background-color`, `transform`, `opacity`.
* **Tip:** You can use the keyword `all` to animate all eligible properties.

**2. `transition-duration`**
* **What it does:** Sets how long the animation should last.
* **Example:** `0.5s` (for 0.5 seconds) or `500ms` (for 500 milliseconds). You must include a time unit!

**3. `transition-timing-function`**
* **What it does:** Defines the speed curve of the animation.
* **Common values:**
  * `ease`: Starts slow, gets fast, then ends slow. (This is the default).
  * `linear`: The animation proceeds at a constant speed.
  * `ease-in-out`: Starts slow and ends slow, with the middle being fast.

**4. `transition-delay`**
* **What it does:** Specifies a delay before the animation starts.
* **Example:** `1s` (the animation will wait for 1 second before beginning).
---

**Syntax:** `transition: [property] [duration] [timing-function] [delay];`\
**Example:** This code will make the background color change to blue over 0.5 seconds with an ease-in-out timing function.

```css
.box {
  background-color: red;
  transition: background-color 0.5s ease-in-out;
}

.box:hover {
  background-color: blue;
}
```

pages.title: CSS transform
pages.content:
- You've learned how to create smooth transitions, but what if you want to animate a button lifting up or an image spinning? That's where the powerful `transform` property comes in.
- The `transform` property lets you change the shape, size, and position of an element in 2D or 3D space. It's special because it does this **without affecting the layout of surrounding elements**.

---
**Core Functions**\
**1. `scale()`**
* **What it does:** Changes the size of an element.
* **Example:** `transform: scale(1.1);` makes an element 10% larger.
* `transform: scale(0.8);` makes it 20% smaller.

**2. `translate()`**
* **What it does:** Moves an element from its original position.
* **Example:**
  * `transform: translateX(20px);` moves it 20 pixels to the right.
  * `transform: translateY(-5px);` moves it 5 pixels up.

**3. `rotate()`**
* **What it does:** Rotates an element clockwise around its center.
* **Example:** `transform: rotate(45deg);` rotates it by 45 degrees.
* You can use negative values for a counter-clockwise rotation.

---
**Putting It All Together**
- You can combine multiple `transform` functions in a single line. The browser applies them in the order they are written.
- **Example:** This code makes an element 10% larger and rotates it by 5 degrees at the same time.
```css
.box {
  transform: scale(1.1) rotate(5deg);
}
```
---
- `transform` is almost always used with the `transition` property you just learned. This is how you create smooth, non-instant animations.

```css
.box {
  transition: transform 0.3s ease-in-out;
}

.box:hover {
  transform: scale(1.1) rotate(5deg);
}
```

pages.title: Introduction to Responsiveness
pages.content:
A **responsive website** automatically adjusts its size and layout so it looks good on **any device** — big desktop screens, tablets, or small mobile phones.

**Why is it important?**
* People use different devices to browse the web.
* A responsive website makes sure **everyone has a good experience**, no matter what screen size they use.

---
**See it in action**


  
  



---
**How do we make websites responsive?**
- We use **CSS techniques** like:
* *Responsive units* (flexible sizes)
* *Media queries* (change styles for different screen sizes)

Don't worry, we'll learn these step by step in the next pages.

pages.title: Responsiveness in the Browser
pages.content:
- In this video, I'll show you how to **check responsiveness in the browser** using the **Inspect tool**.

- We start with our responsive page already built. On a desktop screen, the layout looks like two columns side by side.

- Now, I right-click anywhere on the page and select **Inspect**. From here, I click the small **Toggle Device Toolbar icon** — it looks like a phone and tablet.

- Once this mode is active, I can test how the page looks on different screen sizes. If I choose a smaller device, like an iPhone, you can see that the two columns automatically stack on top of each other. If I switch to a larger screen, like an iPad or a desktop, the layout shifts back into two columns.

- This is the main workflow developers use to **simulate multiple devices without needing the actual hardware**. It's an easy way to confirm that your media queries and responsive styles are working correctly.

- By resizing the viewport and switching between devices, you can make sure your site adapts well to desktops, tablets, and mobiles — all directly from your browser.
